items.prompt: A memcached-style cluster grows from 10 to 11 nodes every evening; with hash % N the database melts from cache misses each time.
items.why: Node count changes and % N remaps almost every key → place keys on a ring so only ~K/N keys move.

items.prompt: A stateless web tier of 12 identical servers needs incoming HTTP requests spread evenly.
items.why: Stateless: any server can handle any request, so a plain load balancer (round robin / least connections) is enough. No key affinity is needed.

items.prompt: A user table is too large for one database; you must choose how to split it and which column to split on.
items.why: 'How do I split the data and on what key' is the sharding decision. Consistent hashing is just one way to place the hash partitions later.

items.prompt: In a peer-to-peer key-value store without a coordinator, every client must compute which 3 nodes hold a key, and nodes join and leave often.
items.why: No central directory, frequent membership changes and R replicas → hash ring with a preference list of the next R distinct nodes.

items.prompt: Reads must survive the loss of any single storage node, so each record needs copies on other machines.
items.why: Surviving node loss is about keeping copies → replication. The ring may choose where the copies go, but the requirement is redundancy.

items.prompt: On a 4-node cache ring with one point per node, node B owns 55% of the keys and runs hot, while another node owns 8%.
items.why: Uneven arcs on the ring → add virtual nodes (many points per server) so ownership averages out.

items.prompt: Each chat connection server keeps in-memory state for its users; when servers are added, as few users as possible should have to reconnect elsewhere.
items.why: Stateful key → server affinity that must survive membership changes with minimal movement → consistent hashing of user id.
